question: The Oliver McGowan Mandatory Training on Learning Disability and Autism was made a statutory requirement for Care Quality Commission (CQC) registered health and social care providers under which piece of legislation?
rationale: Section 181 of the Health and Care Act 2022 introduced the requirement that CQC-registered providers ensure staff receive learning disability and autism training appropriate to their role; the Oliver McGowan Mandatory Training is the government's preferred programme to meet this.
source: NHS England - Oliver McGowan Mandatory Training

question: The Oliver McGowan Mandatory Training on Learning Disability and Autism is delivered across how many tiers?
rationale: The training has two tiers: Tier 1 for staff needing general awareness, and Tier 2 for staff who may provide care and support for people with a learning disability and autistic people. Both share the same eLearning; Tier 2 adds a full day of face-to-face training.
source: Skills for Care - Oliver McGowan Mandatory Training

scenario: A ward manager is deciding which tier of Oliver McGowan training a clinical nurse who directly cares for autistic inpatients should complete.
question: Which tier of the Oliver McGowan Mandatory Training is intended for staff who provide direct care and support to people with a learning disability and autistic people?
rationale: Tier 2 is for staff who may need to provide care and support; it includes the eLearning plus a one-day face-to-face session co-delivered with experts with lived experience. Tier 1 is for general awareness only.
source: National Autistic Society - Tier 2 Oliver McGowan Training

question: A distinctive feature of the Oliver McGowan Mandatory Training is that the interactive and face-to-face sessions are co-delivered by which group of people?
options: Experts by experience - a person with a learning disability and an autistic person - alongside a facilitator
rationale: The training is co-delivered by people with lived experience: a person with a learning disability and an autistic person, working with a facilitator. This co-production is central to the programme's design.
source: NHS England - Oliver McGowan Mandatory Training

question: Under the Equality Act 2010, health and care providers have a legal duty to make what for disabled people, including people with a learning disability?
rationale: The Equality Act 2010 places an anticipatory duty on organisations, including hospitals and GP surgeries, to make reasonable adjustments to remove barriers disabled people face in accessing services.
source: GOV.UK - Reasonable adjustments: a legal duty

scenario: An autistic patient is admitted to a mental health ward. Staff want a patient-held document summarising his needs, likes, dislikes and how he communicates.
question: What is the name of the patient-held, personalised document that captures key information about a person with a learning disability or autism and their needs to support reasonable adjustments in hospital?
rationale: A hospital passport is a patient-held, personalised record of what a person with a learning disability or autism needs, helping staff make reasonable adjustments and understand the individual quickly.

question: By which date must all publicly funded NHS and adult social care services be able to share, write to and read from the national Reasonable Adjustment Digital Flag?
rationale: NHS England states that all NHS and other publicly-funded health and social care services must be able to share, write to and read from the Reasonable Adjustment Digital Flag by 30 September 2026.
source: NHS England - Reasonable adjustment digital flag

scenario: A patient with a learning disability repeatedly bangs their head. Staff assume this is simply part of their learning disability and do not investigate further; the patient actually has a painful dental abscess.
question: This failure to investigate a physical cause because symptoms were attributed to the person's learning disability is an example of what?
rationale: Diagnostic overshadowing is attributing physical or mental health symptoms to a person's learning disability or autism rather than considering a separate new illness, which delays diagnosis and treatment.

question: What does the abbreviation STOMP stand for in the context of people with a learning disability and autistic people?
options: Stopping Over-Medication of People with a learning disability, autism or both
rationale: STOMP stands for Stopping Over-Medication of People with a learning disability, autism or both. It is a national NHS England programme to reduce inappropriate prescribing of psychotropic medicines.

question: Which type of medication is STOMP (Stopping Over-Medication of People with a learning disability, autism or both) particularly concerned with reducing when prescribed inappropriately?
rationale: STOMP focuses on reducing the inappropriate prescribing of psychotropic medicines, including antipsychotics and antidepressants, often used to manage behaviour without a clear clinical justification.

question: STOMP is not an anti-medication campaign. Which statement best describes its actual aim?
options: To ensure medicines are used in the right way, reviewed regularly and optimised, so people stay well and have a good quality of life
To stop all people with a learning disability from ever taking any medication
To replace all medicines with talking therapies only
To transfer prescribing responsibility solely to families
rationale: NHS England is explicit that STOMP and STAMP are not anti-medication; they aim to ensure the right use, review and optimisation of medication so people stay well and have a good quality of life.

question: The paediatric programme that runs alongside STOMP to ensure children and young people get the right medication for the right reason is known by which abbreviation?
rationale: STAMP stands for Supporting Treatment and Appropriate Medication in Paediatrics, the sister programme to STOMP for autistic children and young people and those with a learning disability.

question: What does LeDeR stand for in NHS England's programme to improve care for people with a learning disability and autistic people?
options: Learning from Lives and Deaths - people with a learning disability and autistic people
rationale: LeDeR stands for Learning from Lives and Deaths - people with a learning disability and autistic people. It reviews the care people received to identify learning and reduce health inequalities and premature deaths.
source: NHS England - Learning from lives and deaths (LeDeR)

question: What is the main purpose of the LeDeR (Learning from Lives and Deaths) programme?
options: To learn from the care people received in order to improve services and reduce health inequalities and premature deaths
To prosecute individual clinicians for errors
To decide compensation payments for families
To register every birth of a child with a learning disability
rationale: LeDeR is a service-improvement programme that reviews the health and social care of people with a learning disability and autistic people who have died, to identify good practice and where improvements are needed. It is not a disciplinary or compensation process.
source: NHS England - Learning from lives and deaths (LeDeR)

scenario: A person with a learning disability aged 25 dies on your ward. A colleague asks who is allowed to report the death to LeDeR.
question: Who can notify a death to the LeDeR (Learning from Lives and Deaths) programme?
options: Anyone can notify a death via the online LeDeR system
Only the person's next of kin
rationale: NHS England states that anyone can notify a death to the online LeDeR system. Reviews cover people with a learning disability and autistic people who have died aged 18 and above.
source: NHS England - Learning from lives and deaths (LeDeR)

question: From what age is a person on their GP's learning disability register normally invited for an annual health check?
rationale: Anyone aged 14 or over with a learning disability who is on their GP practice's learning disability register should be invited for a free annual health check.

question: To be invited for an annual health check, a person with a learning disability normally needs to be recorded where?
options: On their GP practice's learning disability register
rationale: Invitations for annual health checks are sent to people aged 14 and over who are on their GP practice's learning disability register. A formal clinical diagnosis is not always required for the GP to add someone to the register.

question: Annual health checks for people with a learning disability are important largely because this group experiences what compared with the general population?
options: Poorer health and higher rates of avoidable, premature death
rationale: People with a learning disability experience significant health inequalities and die earlier than the general population, often from avoidable causes. Annual health checks help find and treat problems early.

scenario: An autistic patient becomes distressed on a busy ward with bright lights, alarms and constant noise.
question: Which reasonable adjustment is most appropriate to address this patient's sensory needs?
options: Reduce sensory triggers, for example by lowering noise and lighting or offering a quieter space
Increase the number of staff talking to them at once
Turn all the lights up brighter
Move them to the busiest part of the ward
rationale: Many autistic people experience sensory sensitivities. Reducing triggers such as noise and bright lighting, or providing a low-stimulation space, is a recognised reasonable adjustment that reduces distress.

scenario: A patient with a learning disability struggles to understand written appointment letters full of medical jargon.
question: Under the Accessible Information Standard, which communication adjustment would be most appropriate?
options: Provide information in an accessible format such as easy read
Send longer letters with more technical detail
rationale: The Accessible Information Standard requires services to identify and meet people's information and communication needs, for example by providing easy read materials for people with a learning disability.

question: The Accessible Information Standard, which requires NHS services to meet the communication needs of people with a disability, impairment or sensory loss, has been mandatory for NHS and publicly funded adult social care organisations since which date?
rationale: From 1 August 2016 all organisations providing NHS or publicly funded adult social care have been legally required to follow the Accessible Information Standard, under section 250 of the Health and Social Care Act 2012.

question: Under the Mental Capacity Act 2005, what must you assume about an adult unless it is established otherwise?
options: That they have capacity to make the decision
That the doctor should always decide
rationale: The first principle of the Mental Capacity Act 2005 is the presumption of capacity: every adult must be assumed to have capacity to make a decision unless it is proved otherwise.
source: SCIE - Mental Capacity Act 2005 at a glance

scenario: A patient with a learning disability makes a decision that staff think is unwise.
question: Under the Mental Capacity Act 2005, how should staff regard a person who makes what appears to be an unwise decision?
options: An unwise decision alone does not mean the person lacks capacity
A best interests decision must immediately be made for them
Their learning disability proves they cannot decide
rationale: A core principle of the Mental Capacity Act 2005 is that a person is not to be treated as unable to make a decision merely because it is unwise. Capacity cannot be assumed to be absent because of a diagnosis such as a learning disability.
source: SCIE - Mental Capacity Act 2005 at a glance

question: The Autism Act 2009 is historically significant in England because it was the first law of its kind. What made it unique?
options: It was the first disability-specific piece of legislation in England
It abolished the Mental Health Act
It removed the need for reasonable adjustments
rationale: The Autism Act 2009 was the first ever disability-specific law in England. It placed a duty on the Secretary of State to publish and keep under review an autism strategy and to issue statutory guidance.
source: House of Commons Library - Autism policy and services

question: Which combination best reflects the recognised NHS definition of a learning disability?
options: A significantly reduced ability to understand new or complex information and learn new skills, with reduced ability to cope independently, which started before adulthood
A physical disability acquired in old age
A short-term difficulty caused by tiredness or stress
A specific difficulty with reading only, such as dyslexia
rationale: The NHS definition of a learning disability includes impaired intelligence (reduced ability to understand new or complex information and learn new skills), impaired social functioning (reduced ability to cope independently), with onset before adulthood. A specific learning difficulty such as dyslexia is not the same as a learning disability.
